stat-01.title: Types of Data
explain: **Statistics** is the discipline that collects and organizes data, finds patterns in it, and draws conclusions under uncertainty. All six lessons in this trunk use only hypothetical data.

Statistics starts with **data**. Each row is one **observation unit** (a person, a shop, a date, and so on), and each column is a **variable** that describes that unit (height, class, number of siblings, and so on). A variable is a characteristic whose value can differ from one unit to another.

Student 5 is in class 2, height 171.3, 3 siblings.

explain: Variables come in two broad kinds. A **categorical** variable has values that are labels, and a **numerical** variable has values that are numbers which can be counted or measured. Whether a variable is a label or a number matters because it determines which calculations make sense. An average of blood types is meaningless, but an average of heights is meaningful.

- **Nominal**: unordered labels. Examples: blood type, region of residence.
- **Ordinal**: labels with an order. Examples: letter grades, satisfaction levels. There is an order, but the gaps between levels cannot be assumed to be equal.
- **Discrete**: numbers that can be counted one by one. Examples: number of siblings, number of visits.
- **Continuous**: numbers that can be measured to any fraction of a unit. Examples: height, commuting time.

stat-02.title: Summarizing Data
explain: It is hard to look at a large amount of data one value at a time. So we summarize data with a few values that represent it. These are called **measures of central tendency**, and there are three typical ones.

- **Mean**: add up all the values and divide by the number of values. If the values are $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$, then $\bar{x} = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n}{n}$.
- **Median**: the middle value when the values are arranged in order of size. If the number of values is even, it is the average of the two middle values.
- **Mode**: the value that occurs most often.

The three values respond differently when the data are skewed to one side. When one very large value is mixed in, the mean is pulled strongly upward, but the median barely changes. So when there are extreme values, the median is often the more trustworthy representative value.

When you want to see the shape of the data rather than a list of numbers, use a **histogram**. Divide the range of values into **intervals** of equal width, and draw a bar for each interval whose height shows how many values fall inside it. The bars touch because the intervals are connected. In this lesson, an interval includes its left endpoint and excludes its right endpoint.

The counts written on the bars are: 0 to 10 minutes, 1; 10 to 20 minutes, 5; 20 to 30 minutes, 2; 30 to 40 minutes, 1; 40 to 50 and 50 to 60 minutes, no bar; 60 to 70 minutes, 1.

stat-03.title: Spread of Data
explain: Even when the means are the same, data can look very different. A quantity that describes whether the values cluster tightly around the average or are spread far from it is called **spread** (dispersion).

explain.alt: Dot plot of two groups (hypothetical data). The horizontal scale runs from 0 to 10 in steps of 2. Row A has dots at 4 (1 dot), 5 (3 dots, stacked upward), and 6 (1 dot). Row B has one dot each at 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9. Both rows have a dashed vertical line at 5, labeled 'mean 5'.
explain.caption: The two groups have the same mean of 5, but their spreads are very different.

explain: The simplest measure of spread is the **range**. $\text{범위} = \text{최댓값} - \text{최솟값}$. It is easy to compute, but it looks at only the largest and smallest values.

To reflect every value, look at how far each value lies from the mean, that is, its **deviation**. The deviation is $x_i - \bar{x}$. But if you simply add up the deviations, positive and negative values cancel and the sum is always 0. So we square the deviations and average them. The result is the **variance**.
$$\text{분산} = \dfrac{(x_1 - \bar{x})^2 + (x_2 - \bar{x})^2 + \cdots + (x_n - \bar{x})^2}{n}$$

The variance is in squared units, which is not intuitive. The positive square root of the variance is the **standard deviation**. It is in the original units, so it is easier to read. $\text{표준편차} = \sqrt{\text{분산}}$. The larger the standard deviation, the more widely the values are spread out.

As a side note, the formula above has $n$ in the denominator. When estimating a population variance from a sample, some methods use $n - 1$ instead. In this lesson we use only the definition above, which divides by $n$ over the whole data set.

stat-04.title: Basics of Probability
explain: **Probability** expresses how likely an uncertain event is as a number between 0 and 1. 0 means the event never happens, and 1 means it always happens.
When all outcomes can be regarded as equally likely, the probability of an event $A$ is:
$$P(A) = \dfrac{A \text{가 일어나는 경우의 수}}{\text{가능한 모든 경우의 수}}$$

- The probability that a fair coin lands heads on one toss is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
- The probability that a die shows an even number on one roll is $\dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

**Counting outcomes** is also needed. When choices are made in successive stages, multiply. With 3 shirts and 4 pairs of pants, there are $3 \times 4 = 12$ ways to get dressed. This is the **multiplication rule**.

If the result of one toss does not affect the next, the two events are called **independent**. The probability that independent events all occur is the product of their individual probabilities. The probability of heads on both of two tosses of a fair coin is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

stat-05.title: Sampling and Estimation
explain: The whole group we want to know about is called the **population**, and the part we actually survey is the **sample**. For example, if we want to know the average sleep time of all high school students in a country but cannot survey all of them, we survey only some.

- A population value (such as the mean) is called a **parameter**. It is usually an unknown true value.
- A value computed from the sample is called a **statistic**. The sample mean $\bar{x}$ is an example.
- Guessing a parameter from a statistic is called **estimation**.

A sample changes each time it is drawn, so the sample mean is not exactly equal to the population mean. This difference is called **sampling error**. It cannot be avoided because it arises from chance, but it generally shrinks as the sample gets larger. How much the sample mean fluctuates is expressed by the **standard error**. If the population standard deviation is $\sigma$ and the sample size is $n$, then:
$$\text{표준오차} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$
So even if the sample size is quadrupled, the standard error only halves. Improving precision has a cost.

**Bias** is a different problem from sampling error. It means the way the sample was drawn systematically skews the estimate in one direction. For example, if we survey people only in front of a library to estimate 'the reading habits of people in this area', people who like books are over-represented, and the reading amount is inflated. No matter how large the sample, bias does not go away. **Random sampling**, in which everyone in the population has an equal chance of being selected, is the basic way to prevent bias.

stat-06.title: Correlation and Causation
explain: To examine the relationship between two variables, draw a **scatter plot**. Each unit is one dot: one variable goes on the horizontal axis and the other on the vertical axis.

explain.alt: Three scatter plots, A, B, and C (hypothetical data, 10 points each). Higher on the page means a larger y, and further right means a larger x. In A, the points line up rising from lower left to upper right. In B, the points line up falling from upper left to lower right. In C, the points are scattered evenly within a square with no clear direction.
explain.caption: The three scatter plots A, B, and C show different relationships.

explain: When one variable tends to increase as the other increases, this is a **positive correlation**. When one variable tends to decrease as the other increases, it is a **negative correlation**. When there is no clear tendency, we say there is **little or no correlation**.

The strength of a relationship is summarized by a single number, the **correlation coefficient** $r$. $r$ is always between $-1$ and $1$. The sign shows the direction, and the absolute value shows how close the points are to a straight line. When $r$ is near 1, the correlation is strong and positive; near $-1$, strong and negative; near 0, there is no strong linear relationship.

The most important caution is this: **a correlation does not mean that one causes the other.** Suppose that in a hypothetical seaside town, days with high ice cream sales also had many swimming accidents. Did ice cream cause the accidents? A third factor, a **confounding variable** (here, hot weather), may affect both.

explain.alt: Arrow diagram. Green arrows run from the top box, 'Very hot weather', to the lower-left box, 'Ice cream sales', and to the lower-right box, 'Number of swimming accidents'. Between the two lower boxes is a dashed line with a question mark. Below the diagram it reads 'Both rise together, but we cannot conclude that one causes the other' and '(green arrows: candidate causes; dashed line: unconfirmed relationship)'.

explain: To claim causation, a correlation alone is not enough. We need a design such as controlling for other factors, or an **experiment** in which subjects are randomly divided and only one group receives the treatment. Correlation is the observation that two things move together; causation is the claim that changing one changes the other.

stat-07.title: Binomial and Poisson Distributions
explain: Questions such as 'What is the probability of 7 or more heads in 10 coin tosses?' or 'What is the probability that more than 3 customers arrive in an hour?' cannot be answered by counting cases every time. Chance events with the same structure follow the same **probability distribution**. Learning the two basic discrete distributions, the binomial and the Poisson, lets many such questions be solved with formulas.

**이항분포** $B(n, p)$: 성공확률 $p$인 독립 시행을 $n$번 할 때 성공 횟수 $X$의 분포다. $$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$$ $\binom{n}{k}$는 $n$번 중 성공할 자리 $k$개를 고르는 경우의 수, 나머지는 그 한 가지 배치의 확률이다. 평균 $np$, 분산 $np(1-p)$이다. 조건은 ① 시행 횟수 고정 ② 각 시행은 성공/실패 둘 중 하나 ③ 성공확률 일정 ④ 시행끼리 독립이다.

**포아송분포** $\text{Pois}(\lambda)$: 일정한 시간·공간에서 드물게 일어나는 사건의 횟수 분포다. $$P(X = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}$$ $\lambda$는 평균 횟수이고, **평균과 분산이 모두 $\lambda$**인 것이 특징이다. 콜센터 전화, 웹사이트 접속, 인쇄물의 오타 수가 대표적 예다. 조건은 사건들이 서로 독립이고, 아주 짧은 구간에 두 번 일어날 확률이 무시할 만하며, 단위 구간당 평균 발생률이 일정하다는 것이다.

The two distributions are connected. When $n$ is large and $p$ is small so that $np = \lambda$ is a moderate size, $B(n, p) \approx \text{Pois}(\lambda)$. For example, the number of defective items among 1000 parts with a defect rate of 0.002 can be approximated by a Poisson distribution with $\lambda = 2$, which is much easier to compute.

Choosing the right distribution is a more important first step than the calculation. If there is an upper bound on the number of times, use the binomial; if you count how often something happens with no upper bound, the Poisson is natural. You should also check the assumptions against the data. If you assume a Poisson distribution but the actual variance is much larger than the mean (**overdispersion**), the events are clustering together.

Limitation: the independence assumption of the binomial fails when sampling without replacement. If the population is small and the drawn items are not returned, the success probability changes at each draw (the hypergeometric distribution). However, if the population is large enough compared with the sample (roughly 20 times or more), the binomial approximation is acceptable.

stat-08.title: The Normal Distribution and Standardization
explain: Measurement error, height, test scores, sample means: many different quantities show a symmetric, bell-shaped distribution. This distribution is the **normal distribution**, and most of statistical inference takes place on it. Why it is so common is explained by the central limit theorem in the next lesson.

The normal distribution $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is completely determined by two parameters, the mean $\mu$ and the standard deviation $\sigma$. Its density function is $\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}$, and the area under the curve gives probabilities. Because it is a continuous distribution, the probability at a single point is 0, and only probabilities over intervals are meaningful.

모든 정규분포는 **표준화**로 하나의 표준정규분포 $N(0, 1)$로 바꿀 수 있다: $$Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}$$ $Z$값은 "평균에서 표준편차 몇 개만큼 떨어졌는가"를 뜻한다. 서로 다른 단위나 척도의 값을 비교할 때도 쓴다. 평균 70·표준편차 10인 시험의 85점($z = 1.5$)이 평균 60·표준편차 20인 시험의 85점($z = 1.25$)보다 상대적으로 더 높다.

explain.alt: Standard normal distribution curve. The horizontal axis z has tick marks from −3 to 3. The region between −1.96 and 1.96 is shaded and labeled 'central area 0.95', and each tail is labeled 0.025.

explain: Reference values to remember: about 68% of values fall within ±1σ of the mean, about 95% within ±2σ, and about 99.7% within ±3σ (the **68-95-99.7 rule**). More precisely, as the figure shows, $-1.96 \le Z \le 1.96$ covers 0.95. This 1.96 is used directly in the 95% confidence interval of stage 3 and in the two-sided test at a 5% significance level.

Limitation: real data are rarely exactly normal. Data skewed to one side, such as income, housing prices, or waiting times, and financial returns with heavy tails, will seriously underestimate the probability of extreme values if approximated by a normal distribution. Check the shape with a histogram or a normal probability plot before using the data.

stat-09.title: The Law of Large Numbers and the Central Limit Theorem
explain: Opinion polls ask only about a thousand people out of tens of millions, yet guarantee the error to within a few percentage points. A single sample mean fluctuates with chance, so how can such a guarantee be made? The answer is that **the sample mean is itself a random variable, and its distribution can be known**.

Draw a sample of size $n$ independently from the population and compute its mean $\bar{X}$. From the properties of expectation and variance (Mathematics, Stage 4), $E[\bar{X}] = \mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\bar{X}) = \sigma^2/n$. The standard deviation of the sample mean, $$SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$ is called the **standard error**. Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error, which means that doubling the precision costs four times as much.

**Law of large numbers**: as $n$ grows, $\bar{X}$ approaches $\mu$, because the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{n} \to 0$. This means the average settles down. It does not mean that 'heads came up often, so tails is due next' (the **gambler's fallacy**). Each trial remains independent.

explain.alt: Two graphs, one above the other. (a) The population distribution has mean 50 and standard deviation 10, and is skewed to the right. (b) The distribution of the means of samples of size 25 is a narrow bell shape symmetric around 50. The horizontal axis tick marks of both graphs are the same: 30, 50, 70, 90.

explain: **Central limit theorem**: regardless of the shape of the population distribution (provided its variance is finite), when $n$ is large enough, the distribution of $\bar{X}$ is close to a **normal distribution** $N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$. As in graph (a), even from a skewed population, the result in graph (b) is a narrow, symmetric bell shape. This is why the normal distribution is so common: sums and averages of many small factors tend to be approximately normal.

Limitations: 'large enough $n$' depends on the shape of the population. If the population is nearly symmetric, $n = 15$ may be enough, but if it is strongly skewed or has frequent extreme values, several hundred may be needed. Also, the central limit theorem is about the distribution of **sample means**. Even as the sample grows, the distribution of the **individual observations** keeps the shape of the population. And if independent sampling is violated (for example, surveying several people from the same household), the standard error formula understates the actual uncertainty.

stat-10.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation: The Parameter That Makes the Data Most Plausible
explain: You toss a coin 10 times and get 7 heads. If asked to estimate the heads probability $p$ as a single number, most people answer 0.7. That is intuitively right. But in more complex models intuition does not work. The **maximum likelihood estimator** (MLE) turns the reason for 'why 0.7' into a principle.

Consider the probability of the observed data when the parameter is $\theta$, viewed as a function of $\theta$, and call it the **likelihood function** $L(\theta)$. Probability looks at 'the data, given the parameter', while likelihood looks at 'the parameter, given the data'. They are two faces of the same expression. Maximum likelihood estimation takes as the estimate the value that **maximizes $L(\theta)$ over $\theta$**.

In the coin example, $L(p) = \binom{10}{7}p^7(1-p)^3$. To make the product easier to handle, take the logarithm: $\ell(p) = 7\ln p + 3\ln(1-p) + $ constant. Differentiating and setting the result to zero gives $\frac{7}{p} - \frac{3}{1-p} = 0$, so $\hat{p} = 0.7$. In general, if there are $n$ trials and $k$ successes, $\hat{p} = k/n$. Taking the logarithm does not change the location of the maximum, because the logarithm is an increasing function.

By the same method, the MLE of the mean of a normal distribution is the sample mean $\bar{x}$, and the MLE of the Poisson $\lambda$ is also the sample mean. For the exponential distribution (with mean waiting time $1/\lambda$), the MLE of $\lambda$ is $1/\bar{x}$. For complex models that cannot be solved by differentiation, the likelihood is maximized numerically by computer. Logistic regression, survival analysis, and many machine learning models are fitted this way.

Also keep in mind the properties of good estimators. **Unbiasedness**: the expected value equals the true value. **Consistency**: the estimate converges to the true value as $n$ grows. **Efficiency**: the variance is small. The MLE is consistent and efficient for large samples and is approximately normally distributed. But in small samples it can be biased. The MLE of a normal variance, $\frac{1}{n}\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2$, slightly underestimates the true value, so the sample variance that divides by $n-1$ is usually used instead.

Limitation: MLE is meaningful only **under the assumption that the model is correct**. Maximizing a Poisson likelihood for data that are not Poisson gives the 'most plausible wrong answer'. Also, with too little data, extreme estimates result. Three coin tosses that all come up heads give $\hat{p} = 1$, which means 'tails never comes up'.

examples.title: MLE of a Poisson parameter
body: Condition: failure counts over 5 days are 2, 0, 3, 1, 4. Use a Poisson model.
Step 1: $\ell(\lambda) = \sum(x_i\ln\lambda - \lambda) + $ constant $= 10\ln\lambda - 5\lambda$.
Step 2: $\frac{10}{\lambda} - 5 = 0$ gives $\hat{\lambda} = 2$, which equals the sample mean.

stat-11.title: Confidence Intervals: Reporting Uncertainty Together
explain: A single point estimate such as '42% support' does not tell you how reliable the number is. Surveying a thousand people or ten people gives very different meanings. A **confidence interval** is the standard way to report an estimate together with the size of its uncertainty.

In stage 2 we learned that $\bar{X} \approx N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$. Therefore $P(-1.96 \le \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \le 1.96) \approx 0.95$, and solving the inequality for $\mu$ gives $$\bar{x} \pm 1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$ which is the **95% confidence interval**. In general it has the form 'estimate ± critical value × standard error', and the critical value × standard error is called the **margin of error**.

The confidence interval for a population proportion is $\hat{p} \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}$. The standard error is largest when $\hat{p} = 0.5$, so the maximum margin of error for a survey of 1000 people is $1.96\sqrt{0.25/1000} \approx 0.031$, or about ±3.1 percentage points. The '±3.1 percentage point margin of error' reported in poll news comes from this calculation.

When $\sigma$ is unknown, we substitute the sample standard deviation $s$. Because of this extra uncertainty, we use a critical value from the **t distribution** (with $n-1$ degrees of freedom), which has slightly heavier tails than the normal distribution. The smaller $n$ is, the larger the critical value and the wider the interval. When $n$ is 30 or more, the value is nearly 1.96.

**Interpretation matters most.** A '95% confidence interval of [38%, 46%]' does **not** mean that 'the probability that the true value lies in this interval is 95%'. The true value is a fixed number, while the interval changes from sample to sample. The precise meaning is: '**If the interval is constructed repeatedly by this method, about 95% of the resulting intervals contain the true value.**' Raising the confidence level to 99% makes the interval wider, and increasing the sample size makes it narrower.

Limitation: a confidence interval reflects only **the chance error of sampling**. Nonresponse, question wording, and groups missing from the sampling frame, that is, **nonsampling error and bias**, are not reflected at all. A biased survey gives a narrow but wrong interval, no matter how large the sample.

examples.title: Confidence interval for a mean
body: Condition: sample of 100, $\bar{x} = 52$, $\sigma = 10$ (assumed known).
Step 1: $SE = 10/10 = 1$, margin of error $= 1.96$.
Step 2: 95% confidence interval $[50.04, 53.96]$. At 99%, using the critical value 2.576, the interval widens to $[49.42, 54.58]$.

Step 2: margin of error $\approx 0.048$, so the 95% confidence interval is about $[0.352, 0.448]$.

stat-12.title: Hypothesis Testing: p-values, Errors, and Power
explain: Does the new teaching method raise test scores? Does the new process reduce defects? Even when the data show a difference, we must judge whether it is a real effect or chance. **Hypothesis testing** is a procedure that judges by calculating how likely such data would be if chance alone were operating.

First, set up two hypotheses. The **null hypothesis** $H_0$ is the reference state we try to refute, such as 'no effect, no difference'. The **alternative hypothesis** $H_1$ is what we want to support. Then find the distribution of the **test statistic** under the assumption that $H_0$ is true. For a test of a mean, $z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$.

The **p-value** is the probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of observing a result as extreme as or more extreme than the one obtained. If the p-value is smaller than the pre-chosen **significance level** $\alpha$ (commonly 0.05), we reject $H_0$. In a two-sided test, $|z| > 1.96$ means $p < 0.05$. Caution: the p-value is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true. It is the probability of the data under the assumption that $H_0$ is true.

There are two kinds of error in these decisions. **Type I error**: rejecting $H_0$ when it is true (a false alarm), with probability $\alpha$. **Type II error**: when $H_1$ is true, failing to reject $H_0$ (missing a real effect), with probability $\beta$. **Power** $1 - \beta$ is the probability of detecting a real effect when it exists. Other things being equal, reducing $\alpha$ increases $\beta$. The reliable way to reduce both errors together is to **increase the sample size**.

Factors that determine power: sample size (larger gives higher power), the size of the true effect (larger gives higher power), the spread of the data $\sigma$ (smaller gives higher power), and the significance level $\alpha$ (larger gives higher power). Calculating how many participants are needed to detect an effect of a given size with 80% probability, at the design stage, is called a **power analysis**.

Limitations and misuse: ① 'Not significant' is not evidence of 'no effect'; the power may simply have been low. ② With very large samples, even practically meaningless small differences become significant, so **the effect size and confidence intervals should be reported together**. ③ If many hypotheses are tested and only the significant ones are reported, false discoveries abound (**multiple comparisons**, or p-hacking). Testing 20 hypotheses, even when no effect exists, will on average produce one with $p < 0.05$.

examples.title: z test
body: Condition: the existing mean is $\mu_0 = 70$, $\sigma = 12$. A class taught with the new method has $n = 36$ and $\bar{x} = 74$. Two-sided test, $\alpha = 0.05$.
Step 2: $|z| = 2 > 1.96$, so reject $H_0$. The two-sided p-value is about 0.046. However, whether an effect of 4 points is practically meaningful must be judged separately.

examples.title: The danger of multiple comparisons
body: Condition: 20 indicators with no actual effect are each tested independently at $\alpha = 0.05$.
Step 1: the probability that none is significant is $0.95^{20} \approx 0.358$.

Step 2: the probability that at least one is 'significant' is about 64%. If we report only the significant results without correction, we mistake chance for discovery. A simple correction is to divide $\alpha$ by the number of tests (the Bonferroni correction).

stat-13.title: Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test
explain: So far we have worked with numerical data such as means. But much data are **categorical**, such as blood type, preferred party, or die faces. For categorical data we analyze how many observations fall into each category (frequencies). The basic tool is the **chi-square ($\chi^2$) test**.

The **goodness-of-fit test** asks whether observed frequencies agree with a theoretical proportion. Examples: is the die fair? Does a 3:1 ratio predicted by a genetic law hold? $H_0$: the category proportions equal the theoretical proportions $p_1, \dots, p_k$. If the sample size is $n$, the **expected frequency** of each category is $E_i = np_i$.

검정통계량은 관측 빈도 $O_i$와 기대 빈도의 차이를 모은 $$\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}$$ 이다. 제곱하므로 부호가 사라지고, $E_i$로 나누어 기대가 큰 범주의 차이를 상대적으로 작게 본다. $H_0$가 참이면 이 값은 자유도 $k - 1$인 **카이제곱분포**를 따른다. 범주가 $k$개라도 합계가 $n$으로 고정되어 있어 자유롭게 정할 수 있는 칸이 $k - 1$개이기 때문이다.

The larger the value, the farther the data are from the theory. At significance level 0.05, the critical values are 3.84 for 1 degree of freedom, 5.99 for 2, 7.81 for 3, and 11.07 for 5. If the calculated $\chi^2$ exceeds the critical value, reject $H_0$. The chi-square test is always a **right-tailed** test, because only a large difference is meaningful.

Conditions and limitations: ① the observations must be **independent** (one person should not respond more than once). ② If the expected frequencies are too small (usually when many cells have expected counts below 5), the chi-square approximation becomes poor; combine categories or use an exact test. ③ The calculation must use **frequencies (counts)**. Entering percentages loses the sample size information and gives wrong results. ④ Rejection only means that 'something differs'. To find which category differs, interpret each category's contribution $(O-E)^2/E$ separately.

There is also a historically interesting use. A **too-small** $\chi^2$, that is, data that fit the theory too perfectly, is itself viewed with suspicion. Real data contain random fluctuation, so if the data match the theory perfectly every time, the possibility that the data were 'tidied up' is examined.

Step 2: with 5 degrees of freedom, the critical value is 11.07. Since $13.4 > 11.07$, reject the hypothesis that the die is fair. Most of the contribution (10.0) comes from face 6.

stat-14.title: Contingency Tables and the Chi-Square Test of Independence
explain: Questions such as 'Does the preferred menu differ by gender?' or 'Is smoking related to exercise habits?' ask about the relationship between two categorical variables. Summarize them in a **contingency table** (cross-tabulation) and judge them with the **chi-square test of independence**.

행 변수 $r$개 범주, 열 변수 $c$개 범주의 분할표를 만든다. $H_0$: 두 변수는 독립이다. 독립이면 수학 4단계의 정의에 따라 각 칸의 확률이 행 확률 × 열 확률이다. 그래서 각 칸의 **기대 빈도**는 $$E_{ij} = \frac{(\text{행 합계}_i)(\text{열 합계}_j)}{\text{전체 합계}}$$ 이다. 관측 빈도와 비교하는 통계량은 적합도 검정과 같은 $\chi^2 = \sum\frac{(O - E)^2}{E}$이다.

The degrees of freedom are $(r - 1)(c - 1)$, because once the row totals and column totals are fixed, the last row and last column are determined automatically by the remaining cells. For a 2×2 table the degrees of freedom are 1, and the critical value is 3.84.

The **direction and size** of the association are examined separately from the test. Compare the column proportions within each row (conditional proportions), or, for a 2×2 table, compute the **relative risk** or the **odds ratio**. For example, if 60% of people who exercise and 30% of people who do not exercise eat breakfast, the difference of 30 percentage points is the size of the association.

The chi-square test of independence shows **association**, not **causation**. Also beware of **Simpson's paradox**: when the groups are examined separately, A beats B in every group, but when they are combined, B may appear better. This happens when a hidden third variable has different group sizes and compositions. Get into the habit of splitting the table into strata before combining them.

Limitations: as with the goodness-of-fit test, the observations must be independent and the expected frequencies must be adequate. For paired data, such as the same people surveyed before and after, another method (McNemar's test), not this test, should be used. And with a very large sample, even practically meaningless small differences become significant.

examples.title: Independence test for a 2×2 table
body: Condition: among 100 people who exercise, 60 eat breakfast and 40 do not. Among 100 people who do not exercise, 40 eat breakfast and 60 do not.
Step 1: row totals are 100 and 100, column totals are 100 and 100, and the grand total is 200. Every expected frequency is $100 \times 100/200 = 50$.
Step 2: $\chi^2 = 4 \times \frac{10^2}{50} = 8.0 > 3.84$. Reject the hypothesis of independence. The two habits are related. However, this data cannot tell us which one is the cause.

stat-15.title: One-Way ANOVA: Comparing the Means of Several Groups
explain: We want to compare the crop yields of three fertilizers. Could we run t tests on pairs of groups, three times? As the multiple-comparisons problem from stage 3 shows, the probability of a false discovery then grows. **Analysis of variance** (ANOVA) tests whether the means of several groups are all equal in **a single test**. Despite its name, it compares means, and it does so by comparing **ratios of variances**.

핵심 아이디어는 전체 변동을 두 부분으로 쪼개는 것이다. $$\text{SST} = \text{SSB} + \text{SSW}$$ **집단 간 변동** SSB $= \sum_j n_j(\bar{x}_j - \bar{x})^2$는 집단 평균들이 전체 평균에서 얼마나 떨어져 있는지, **집단 내 변동** SSW $= \sum_j\sum_i(x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2$는 각 집단 안에서 값들이 얼마나 흩어져 있는지를 잰다.

각 변동을 자유도로 나눈 것이 **평균제곱**이다. 집단이 $k$개, 전체 관측이 $N$개면 MSB $=$ SSB$/(k-1)$, MSW $=$ SSW$/(N-k)$이다. 검정통계량은 $$F = \frac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}}$$ 이다. 모든 집단 평균이 같다면($H_0$) 두 평균제곱은 모두 같은 오차 분산을 추정하므로 $F \approx 1$이다. 평균이 다르면 MSB가 커져 $F$가 1보다 훨씬 커진다.

If $H_0$ is true, $F$ follows an **F distribution** with degrees of freedom $(k-1, N-k)$. If the calculated $F$ exceeds the critical value (or the p-value is below $\alpha$), we conclude that at least one group mean differs. The F test does not tell us which groups differ, so after rejection we perform **post hoc tests** (such as Tukey's method) that correct for multiple comparisons.

Intuitively, for the same difference in means, the difference is clearer when the scatter within groups is small. Three groups with means 10, 12, and 14 are clearly different if the values in each group cluster within ±0.5, but hard to distinguish from chance if they scatter by ±10. F is exactly this signal-to-noise ratio.

Assumptions and limitations: ① each group is an independent sample. ② Within each group, the data are approximately normal. ③ The groups have similar variances (homoscedasticity). If the equal-variance assumption is badly violated and the group sizes also differ, the results are hard to trust. Also, if the data are observational rather than experimental, ANOVA alone cannot tell whether the differences between groups come from the treatment or from other factors.

examples.title: Computing F for small data
body: Condition: group A {4, 5, 6}, group B {6, 7, 8}, group C {8, 9, 10}. The group means are 5, 7, and 9, and the overall mean is 7.
Step 1: SSB $= 3(5-7)^2 + 3(7-7)^2 + 3(9-7)^2 = 24$. SSW: each group contributes $1 + 0 + 1 = 2$, for a total of 6.
Step 2: MSB $= 24/2 = 12$, MSW $= 6/6 = 1$, $F = 12$. This exceeds the 0.05 critical value of about 5.14 for (2, 6) degrees of freedom, so reject the hypothesis that all the means are equal.

Step 2: MSW $= 25$, $F = 12/25 = 0.48$. Even with the same differences in means, large noise prevents them from serving as evidence.

stat-16.title: Simple Linear Regression and the Method of Least Squares
explain: In stage 1 we measured how much two variables move together using the correlation coefficient. Regression analysis goes one step further: it expresses **as an equation** the answer to 'when $x$ increases by 1, how much does $y$ change on average?', and it uses $x$ to **predict** $y$.

The **simple linear regression** model is $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \varepsilon_i$. $\beta_1$ is the slope, $\beta_0$ is the intercept, and $\varepsilon_i$ is the error not explained by the straight line. The standard method for choosing from the data the line $\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1x$ is the **method of least squares** (OLS). It picks the line that minimizes the sum of squares of the **residuals** $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$, the vertical distances between the observed values and the line.

제곱합을 $b_0$, $b_1$로 편미분해 0으로 놓으면(수학 3단계) 다음을 얻는다. $$b_1 = \frac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \quad b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}$$ 둘째 식에서 **회귀직선은 항상 평균점 $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$를 지난다**. 기울기는 상관계수와 $b_1 = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$로 연결된다.

explain.alt: Scatter plot with study time x on the horizontal axis (0 to 6) and score y on the vertical axis (0 to 7). The points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), and (5, 6) are plotted, and the least-squares line is drawn as an orange dashed line.

explain: The key to interpretation is the slope. 'For each additional hour of study, the score is higher by 0.8 points on average' is an example of such a reading. The intercept is the predicted value at $x = 0$, but when 0 is outside the range of the data, it often has no meaningful interpretation. Also, **extrapolation**, predicting with an $x$ far outside the range of the data, is risky. At 50 hours of study the model predicts 41.8 points, but there is no evidence that the linear relationship holds that far.

Limitation: the regression slope measures the size of an **association**. Even if the slope from observational data is 0.8, we cannot conclude that adding an hour of study raises the score by 0.8 points. Perhaps diligent students study more and also score higher (confounding). We address this problem with multiple regression in the last lesson of stage 5. Also, OLS squares the residuals, so a single **outlier** can pull the line strongly.

stat-17.title: The Coefficient of Determination and Residual Diagnostics
explain: A regression line can be drawn for any data. We must separately check how well the line explains the data, and whether the straight-line model itself is appropriate. The first question is answered by the **coefficient of determination**, and the second by **residual diagnostics**.

분산분석처럼 $y$의 전체 변동을 쪼갠다. $\text{SST} = \sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2$는 회귀로 설명된 부분 $\text{SSR} = \sum(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2$와 남은 부분 $\text{SSE} = \sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$의 합이다. **결정계수** $$R^2 = \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}} = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}$$ 는 $y$의 변동 중 회귀직선이 설명하는 비율이다. 단순회귀에서는 $R^2 = r^2$이다. $r = 0.6$이면 변동의 36%만 설명한다.

A high $R^2$ does not mean the model is correct. A straight line fitted to a curved relationship can still have a fairly high $R^2$, and two unrelated variables that both increase over time (such as ice cream sales and the population of a country) can also have a high $R^2$. Conversely, even a low $R^2$ can matter when the slope is practically meaningful. In phenomena with inherently large noise, such as human behavior, $R^2 = 0.2$ can be a meaningful finding.

For inference from OLS regression (confidence intervals and tests for the slope) to be valid, assumptions about the errors are needed. ① **Linearity**: the mean relationship is a straight line. ② **Independence**: the errors are independent of each other. ③ **Homoscedasticity**: the variance of the errors is constant regardless of $x$. ④ **Normality**: the errors are approximately normally distributed (especially important for small samples). These assumptions are checked by plotting the residuals.

explain.alt: Two residual-versus-fitted plots. In (a), the points scatter in a band of constant width above and below the horizontal dashed line at 0. In (b), the points move farther and farther from the dashed line as the fitted values increase, forming a funnel shape.

explain: In the ideal **residuals-versus-fitted-values plot**, the points form a random band of constant width around 0, as in (a). A funnel shape, in which the spread grows as the fitted values increase, as in (b), is a **violation of homoscedasticity**. In that case the standard errors are wrong, so confidence intervals and p-values cannot be trusted. Remedies include a log transformation or standard errors that are robust to heteroscedasticity. If the residuals form a U-shaped or inverted-U curve, that is a **violation of linearity**, and the model must be changed, for example by adding a squared term.

stat-18.title: Multiple Regression and Controlling for Confounding Variables
explain: Suppose a simple regression shows that the more coffee people drink, the higher their risk of heart disease. But suppose many heavy coffee drinkers are also smokers. Then the apparent effect of coffee may actually be the effect of smoking. A third variable that affects both the explanatory variable and the outcome is called a **confounding variable**. **Multiple regression** reduces this problem by including several variables together.

The multiple regression model is $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \cdots + \beta_px_p + \varepsilon$. The principle of estimating the coefficients by least squares is the same, but the computation is done with matrices ($\mathbf{b} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf{y}$, Mathematics, Stage 2). Interpretation is the key. The coefficient $b_1$ measures, **holding the other variables fixed**, how a unit increase in $x_1$ changes the average of $y$. This is the effect of that variable after **controlling** for the other variables.

Controlling for a confounder can change a coefficient dramatically. If the coffee slope was strongly positive when coffee was the only variable, but becomes nearly 0 once smoking is included, then most of the original association was produced by smoking as a confounder. The size of this change indicates the extent of the confounding. Conversely, if the coefficient barely changes after controlling, that variable is not the reason for the association.

Which variables to control for is decided by **knowledge of the causal structure**. Confounders, which affect both the cause and the outcome, should be controlled. But controlling for a **mediator** (cause → mediator → outcome) erases part of the effect we want to know. If exercise lowers blood pressure by reducing body weight, then controlling for weight when studying the blood-pressure effect of exercise underestimates that effect. More variables are not always better.

Practical cautions: when explanatory variables are highly correlated (**multicollinearity**), the standard errors of the coefficients become large and the interpretation unstable. Adding a variable **always** increases $R^2$, so we use the **adjusted $R^2$**, which penalizes the number of variables. Categorical variables are entered as 0/1 **dummy variables**.

Limitation: multiple regression controls only for **variables that were measured and included**. Unmeasured confounders remain. That is why regression results from observational data should be read as causal only with great caution. Randomized experiments are the standard for causal inference because, since assignment is by chance, all confounders, measured or not, are on average spread evenly across the groups.

examples.title: Coefficients before and after control (hypothetical data)
body: Condition: the outcome is the number of hospital visits per year. Model 1: visits $= 2.0 + 0.30 \times$ coffee (cups per day). Model 2: visits $= 1.8 + 0.02 \times$ coffee $+ 1.5 \times$ smoking (1 or 0).
Step 1: the coffee coefficient fell from 0.30 to 0.02.

Step 2: when smoking was controlled, the association between coffee and visits nearly disappeared. The original association was mostly produced by smoking as a confounder. At the same coffee consumption, smokers visit an average of 1.5 times more often than non-smokers.

examples.title: Interpreting coefficients and prediction
body: Condition: house price (100 million won) $= 0.5 + 0.03 \times$ area (m²) $- 0.02 \times$ distance to the station (in units of 100 m).

Step 1: holding distance constant, a home with 10 m² more area is 0.3 (100 million won) higher. Holding area constant, each additional 100 m from the station lowers the price by 0.02 (100 million won).
Step 2: for an 80 m² home 500 m (5 units) from the station, the prediction is $0.5 + 2.4 - 0.1 = 2.8$ (100 million won).

stat-19.title: Comprehensive Problem Solving: Analyzing One Dataset from Start to Finish
explain: The first capstone lesson uses the tools from stages 2 to 5, in sequence, on a single hypothetical dataset. Situation: a regional library wants to know how participation in a reading program (participated or did not participate) affects students' reading comprehension scores. The data for 200 students include participation status, a reading comprehension score (0 to 100), and the number of books at home (volumes).

**Step 1 (question and hypotheses)**: convert the question into testable hypotheses. $H_0$: the mean scores of the participating and non-participating groups are equal. $H_1$: they differ. The significance level is set to 0.05 **before** looking at the data. Fixing the analysis plan in advance is the most reliable way to prevent multiple comparisons and p-hacking.

**Step 2 (descriptive statistics and testing)**: the 100 participants averaged 72 points and the 100 non-participants averaged 66 points; both groups have a standard deviation of 15 points. The standard error of the 6-point difference in means is $\sqrt{15^2/100 + 15^2/100} \approx 2.12$, so $z \approx 2.83$ and $p \approx 0.005$, which rejects the null hypothesis. The 95% confidence interval for the difference is $6 \pm 1.96 \times 2.12$, about [1.8, 10.2] points.

**Step 3 (suspecting confounding)**: however, participation was not assigned at random. Students from homes with many books may both participate more and score higher. The number of books at home is a candidate confounder. Suppose we fit the multiple regression score $= b_0 + b_1 \times$ participation $+ b_2 \times$ books (hundreds) and obtain $b_1 = 2.5$ (standard error 2.0) and $b_2 = 3.0$.

**Step 4 (interpretation)**: controlling for the number of books, the participation effect falls from 6 points to 2.5 points, and since $2.5/2.0 = 1.25 < 1.96$, it is no longer significant. Much of the original difference was probably due to differences in home environment. However, it would also be hasty to conclude that 'the program has no effect'. The confidence interval of about [−1.4, 6.4] points shows that the effect could be zero or quite large.

**Step 5 (critique and next steps)**: unmeasured confounders remain, such as learning motivation and parental interest. The most reliable next step is an experiment that **randomly assigns** participation. If an experiment is difficult, improve the design, for example by comparing changes in scores before and after the program. The report should state the effect size, the confidence interval, and both the confounders that were controlled and those that were not.

examples.title: Standard error of a difference in two means
body: Condition: two independent groups, $s_1 = s_2 = 15$, $n_1 = n_2 = 100$.
Step 2: if each group is enlarged to 400 people, $SE = \sqrt{0.5625 + 0.5625} \approx 1.06$, which is half as large.

examples.title: Writing the reporting sentence
body: Poor example: "The reading program raises scores (p < 0.05)."

Good example: "The participating group's mean score was 6 points higher (95% CI 1.8 to 10.2). However, after controlling for the number of books at home, the difference fell to 2.5 points (95% CI −1.4 to 6.4) and was not statistically significant. Because participation was not randomized, the difference is difficult to interpret as a causal effect."

checks.prompt: Arrange the steps of data analysis in the correct order.

Examine the data with descriptive statistics and graphs
Evaluate the difference with a test and a confidence interval
Examine possible confounding and control for it with multiple regression
Report the effect size, the confidence interval, and the limitations together

Much of the original difference is likely explained by the home environment, but whether an effect exists cannot be settled by this data; a randomized experiment or similar design is needed

stat-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Designing an Analysis and Critiquing Statistical Misuse
explain: The final task has two parts. **(a) Design a data analysis** for one question that interests you, and **(b) critique one claim that misuses statistics**. You do not need to collect real data. The key is to plan which data to collect, how to collect them, what analysis to run, and how to interpret the results.

Design framework: ① **Question and hypotheses**: in a testable form. ② **Data collection**: population, sampling method, sample size (considering power), and measurement method. ③ **Analysis method**: a tool suited to the variable types (comparing means: t test or ANOVA; relationships among categories: chi-square; relationships among continuous variables: regression). ④ **Confounding and control**: which variables to measure and control for, and whether random assignment is possible. ⑤ **Reporting plan**: effect size, confidence interval, and limitations.

Common statistical misuses: interpreting correlation as causation, biased samples (self-selected respondents, or surveying only survivors), reporting only p-values while hiding effect sizes, reporting only the significant results after multiple comparisons, extrapolation, graphs with truncated axes that exaggerate differences, reporting only means while hiding a skewed distribution, ignoring base rates (Bayes, Mathematics Stage 4), Simpson's paradox, and confusing percentages with percentage points.

When writing a critique, do not stop at 'it is wrong'. Present **what** the problem is (which assumption was violated), **how the conclusion could change**, and **what data or design would be needed to answer the question properly**. A good critique includes an alternative.
This task is not graded. The text you submit is stored only on this device and can be viewed again under 'My Progress' in 'My Notes'.

examples.title: Model design: sleep time and academic achievement
body: Question: do students with longer weekday sleep have higher end-of-term scores? This is continuous × continuous, so use regression.

Data: students in classes randomly selected from several schools; sleep recorded over one week; scores from a common test. Compute the sample size so that power is 80% if the effect is 2 points per hour.
Confounding: measure study time, home environment, and health status, and control for them in multiple regression. Note the unmeasured motivation as a limitation.
Reporting: the coefficient with its 95% confidence interval, the results of the residual diagnostics, and an explicit statement that 'this is association, not causation'.

examples.title: Model critique: "90% of our app users are satisfied"
body: Problem: if the survey was a pop-up inside the app, only people who keep using it will respond (survivor bias). People who were dissatisfied had already deleted the app.
Change in conclusion: actual satisfaction is likely to be lower than this figure.
Alternative: sample randomly from the full list of registered users (including those who left) and contact them, and report the response rate and the characteristics of non-respondents.

checks.prompt: Match each variable type and question with the appropriate analysis tool.
checks.hint: Check whether the outcome variable is continuous or categorical, and how many groups there are.
checks.explanation: The variable type determines the tool.
pairs: Comparing the average commuting time of students in three departments
Relationship between region of residence (4 places) and preferred mode of transport (3 types)
Judging whether a die is fair

checks.prompt: A graph starts its vertical axis at 95, so that the difference between 98 and 99 looks three times as tall as a bar. What is the name of this misuse, and which response matches it?
checks.hint: The visual size does not match the numerical ratio.
checks.explanation: A bar chart asks readers to judge size by bar length, so truncating the axis exaggerates differences.
options: Multiple-comparisons problem — Bonferroni correction
Exaggerated difference from a truncated axis — start the axis at 0, or clearly mark the truncation and state the actual difference numerically
Simpson's paradox — stratified analysis
Extrapolation — predict only within the range of the data

checks.prompt: A news report says 'support rose from 20% to 25%, a 25% increase.' What is the actual change expressed in percentage points? (%p)
checks.explanation: It is a 5 percentage point increase; in relative terms it is a 5/20 = 25% increase. Confusing the two misleads readers.

checks.prompt: Introduce one statistical claim you would critique, and diagnose in two to four sentences what is wrong with it.
checks.hint: Follow the order of the model critique: problem → change in conclusion → alternative.
checks.explanation: A good critique includes an alternative.
checks.model: I critique the claim that 'students who eat breakfast have higher grades, so breakfast raises grades.' This treats an association in observational data as causation. Economic resources or regular living habits of the household may be confounders that affect both breakfast and grades. So the effect of breakfast may have been exaggerated. A study that measures and controls these variables, or one that randomly assigns breakfast provision, is needed.

checks.prompt: Capstone task: (a) design an analysis of one question that interests you (question and hypotheses, data collection and sample size, analysis tools, control of confounding, and reporting plan), and (b) write a complete critique of the statistical misuse you chose in the previous item, in at least 400 characters.
checks.hint: Fill in design framework items ① to ⑤ in order, and write the critique as problem → change in conclusion → alternative.
checks.explanation: This task is not graded. Use the checklist to improve it yourself.
checklist: I set a testable hypothesis and fixed the significance level in advance
I considered the sampling method and the sample size (power)
I chose an analysis tool suited to the variable types
I wrote down the confounders and how to control them (or random assignment)
I planned to report the effect size, confidence interval, and limitations
